articles.title: Vacinação contra o sarampo: nenhum estado do Brasil atinge meta | G1
articles.standfirst: Cobertura nacional com duas doses da tríplice viral está abaixo de 80%, distante dos 95% necessários para conter a circulação do vírus. Países das Américas enfrentam avanço da doença, com mortes e milhares de casos.
articles.summary: A cobertura da vacinação contra o sarampo está abaixo de 80%, longe dos 95% ideais, enquanto surtos da doença avançam pelas Américas com milhares de casos registrados.
articles.body:
Nenhum estado do Brasil atinge meta de vacinação contra o sarampo; especialistas alertam para risco de novos surtos — Foto: Adobe Stock

O Brasil tenta preservar o status de país livre da circulação endêmica do sarampo, recuperado em novembro de 2024, em um momento em que países vizinhos registram mais de 20 mil casos. O Peru, por exemplo, já tem cerca de 3 mil casos e a Bolívia também vive uma situação de descontrole, conforme destacou ao g1 o diretor do Departamento Nacional de Imunizações (DPNI), Eder Gatti.

Por isso, o foco do Ministério da Saúde neste momento é reforçar a vigilância e intensificar a vacinação com a tríplice viral, que protege contra sarampo, caxumba e rubéola, em municípios que fazem fronteira com o Peru, na região oeste do Amazonas.

Apesar de o país ter a melhor cobertura de vacinação contra o sarampo desde 2016, nenhum estado atingiu ainda a meta de vacinar 95% das crianças menores de 2 anos com duas doses por ano. Este é o índice considerado necessário para impedir a circulação sustentada de um dos vírus mais contagiosos que existem.

No país, a imunização completa com as duas doses da vacina tríplice viral está abaixo de 80%, cenário que preocupa especialistas diante do avanço da doença em países vizinhos.

A primeira dose garante uma imunidade de 94% a 96% contra o sarampo. Já as duas doses garantem proteção acima de 97% contra a doença.

Gatti explicou que, em crianças de até 5 anos, a cobertura da segunda dose chegou a 91% em 2024, ainda também abaixo da meta de 95%. Além disso, o período ideal para a criança ser vacinada com as duas doses é de até os 2 anos de idade.

Este ano, os estados que lideram o índice de cobertura vacinal contra a doença até o momento são o Ceará, com 86,69%; Paraná, com 86,76%, e Minas Gerais com 86,05%.

Os piores índices foram registrados até agora no Amapá, com 63,59%; Pará, com 67,02%; Maranhão, com 69,66% e Rio de Janeiro, com 69,74%.

Já em 2025, os estados que tiveram os melhores índices de cobertura foram o Paraná, com 89,92%; Minas Gerais, com 87,62; Rondônia, com 84,56% e Distrito Federal, com 84,03%. E os piores índices ficaram com o Pará, com 58,25%; Goiás, com 58,59% e Amapá, com 63,02%.

Fonte: Ministério da Saúde — Foto: Arte g1

Casos importados podem provocar novos surtos

Embora o país não registre transmissão sustentada da doença, casos importados continuam sendo identificados e podem provocar novos surtos, especialmente em regiões com baixa cobertura vacinal.

Em 2025, o Brasil registrou 39 casos de sarampo. Em 2026, já são pouco mais de 50, destaca o infectologista Renato Kfouri, vice-presidente da Sociedade Brasileira de Imunizações (SBIm). A maioria das ocorrências deste ano foi registrada no estado de São Paulo, principalmente na capital.

Os números brasileiros contrastam com a situação de países vizinhos e dos Estados Unidos, que enfrentam um dos piores cenários de sarampo das últimas décadas. O país norte-americano já ultrapassou 3,6 mil casos em 2026 e cinco mortes. No início de outubro, Nova York declarou estado de emergência devido ao avanço da doença.

Para os especialistas, a principal preocupação é que a redução da vacinação permita o acúmulo de pessoas suscetíveis à infecção, criando condições para que casos isolados se transformem em surtos.

"Quando a gente atinge mais de 95% da população vacinada, a gente impede que esses casos importados se traduzam por uma transmissão sustentada da doença, mantendo a circulação do vírus aqui. Então a gente precisa não só ter coberturas elevadas, mas também homogêneas, porque bolsões de baixas coberturas podem também ter o mesmo efeito da cobertura não tão ideal", explica Kfouri.

Brasil recuperou certificação de eliminação, mas continua registrando casos

Segundo Kfouri, o último caso autóctone registrado no país (de quem contrai uma doença no próprio território onde vive ou onde o caso foi registrado) ocorreu em junho de 2022, no Amapá.

Isso não significa, porém, que o vírus tenha deixado de representar uma ameaça.

A circulação internacional de pessoas continua trazendo casos para o território brasileiro. São brasileiros que contraem a doença durante viagens ao exterior ou estrangeiros que chegam infectados ao país.

Esses episódios podem provocar pequenas cadeias de transmissão, mesmo sem estabelecer uma circulação contínua do vírus.

Segundo Kfouri, foi o que ocorreu nos casos registrados recentemente no Brasil, com transmissões restritas a pequenos grupos.

Este ano, a maior concentração de casos ocorreu em São Paulo. Segundo o infectologista, o estado está há sete semanas praticamente sem novos registros, mas é necessário observar um período maior para considerar interrompida a transmissão.

O especialista explica ainda que a entrada de novos casos no Brasil é esperada, especialmente diante dos surtos em países das Américas.

"É inexorável a entrada de pessoas com sarampo aqui no país, já que o deslocamento populacional, milhares de pessoas vêm desses países vizinhos diariamente por fronteiras secas, aéreas, rodoviárias", afirma.

Para ele, a diferença entre identificar um caso importado e enfrentar um surto está diretamente relacionada à proteção da população.

A vacinação elevada e distribuída de maneira homogênea é fundamental para evitar que o vírus encontre pessoas suscetíveis suficientes para manter sua transmissão.

O sarampo é uma das doenças infecciosas mais contagiosas que existem. Sua transmissão ocorre pelo ar, por meio da tosse, espirros, fala ou respiração de uma pessoa infectada.

Por causa da facilidade de disseminação do vírus, é necessário que pelo menos 95% da população esteja protegida para impedir sua circulação sustentada.

Esse patamar está relacionado à chamada imunidade coletiva, ou imunidade de rebanho, quando há um número suficiente de pessoas imunizadas para dificultar a transmissão da doença, inclusive protegendo aquelas que não podem receber a vacina.

Quando a cobertura fica abaixo desse nível, aumentam as possibilidades de circulação do vírus.

O problema não se limita aos índices nacionais ou estaduais. Mesmo em regiões com percentuais relativamente elevados, podem existir comunidades com grande concentração de pessoas não vacinadas.

Esses grupos formam os chamados bolsões de suscetibilidade, capazes de favorecer surtos localizados.

Kfouri ressalta que, além de alcançar a meta, é necessário garantir que a vacinação esteja distribuída entre diferentes regiões e grupos populacionais.

A pediatra Flavia Bravo, diretora da Sociedade Brasileira de Imunizações (SBIm), também alerta que reduções aparentemente pequenas na cobertura vacinal podem representar um número expressivo de pessoas desprotegidas.

"A redução da imunização, ainda que pareça uma taxa mínima, tem resultados sem precedentes, como o que estamos vendo. O país criou uma multidão de pessoas suscetíveis e que hoje são crianças e adultos vulneráveis ao vírus", explica Bravo, ao comentar a situação dos Estados Unidos.

Estados Unidos enfrentam pior surto em décadas

A situação norte-americana mostra como a queda na vacinação pode favorecer o retorno de uma doença anteriormente controlada.

Os Estados Unidos registraram mais de 3,6 mil casos de sarampo em 2026 e todas as vítimas não estavam imunizadas. O índice é 59% superior ao total de 2025, que já havia sido o pior ano em décadas.

O cenário é resultado de uma queda prolongada da cobertura vacinal. Em 2011, 21 dos 44 estados norte-americanos com dados disponíveis alcançavam cobertura superior a 95% contra o sarampo. Atualmente, apenas 10 dos 49 estados avaliados mantêm esse patamar.

A queda se intensificou durante a pandemia de Covid-19 e não foi revertida nos anos seguintes.

Entre crianças que ingressaram na pré-escola, a cobertura média da vacina tríplice viral caiu para 92,5%.

Uma análise baseada nos dados dos Centros de Controle e Prevenção de Doenças (CDC) indica que pelo menos 1,7 milhão de crianças deixaram de completar a vacinação contra o sarampo nos últimos anos.

O infectologista Peter Hotez, da National School of Tropical Medicine, do Baylor College of Medicine, no Texas, atribui parte importante dessa redução ao crescimento dos movimentos antivacinação.

"Temos um extenso movimento antivacinação que abrange condados inteiros. Tudo isso resultado do movimento antivacinação e é cada vez mais difícil convencer os pais de que as crianças precisam ser vacinadas", afirma.

Segundo ele, o problema é agravado pela existência de comunidades com cobertura muito baixa, mesmo em estados cujos índices gerais parecem relativamente elevados.

A situação também se reflete nos surtos recentes. Em 5 de outubro, a governadora de Nova York, Kathy Hochul, declarou estado de emergência devido ao aumento de casos de sarampo.

Até 3 de outubro, o estado havia registrado 108 infecções em 2026, das quais 92 ocorreram entre 15 de julho e o início de outubro, principalmente em comunidades rurais com baixa cobertura vacinal.

O decreto ampliou o número de profissionais autorizados a aplicar vacinas e solicitar exames para suspeitas da doença.

Na Pensilvânia, outro estado norte-americano afetado, o decreto de Nova York apontava 977 casos e cinco mortes até 2 de outubro.

Além dos Estados Unidos, Canadá, México e Guatemala enfrentam grandes surtos, segundo Kfouri. Argentina, Bolívia, Peru e Paraguai também registram casos.

Desinformação e baixa percepção do risco dificultam vacinação

Entre os fatores que ajudam a explicar a redução das coberturas vacinais, especialistas destacam a disseminação de informações falsas sobre a segurança dos imunizantes.

Nos Estados Unidos, o presidente Donald Trump e o secretário de Saúde, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., fizeram declarações associando vacinas ao autismo, apesar de não existirem evidências científicas que sustentem essa relação.

A hipótese surgiu a partir de um estudo fraudulento publicado em 1998, posteriormente retirado pela revista científica responsável pela publicação.

Desde então, pesquisas realizadas em diferentes países, acompanhando milhões de crianças, não encontraram relação causal entre vacinação e autismo.

Em agosto, a Organização Mundial da Saúde (OMS) advertiu que as mudanças promovidas na política de vacinação infantil norte-americana contrariavam décadas de evidências científicas.

O diretor-geral da organização, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, reforçou que as vacinas são seguras e não causam autismo.

Uma pesquisa Reuters/Ipsos realizada em setembro também identificou uma redução na confiança dos norte-americanos na vacina contra sarampo, caxumba e rubéola.

Em 2020, 84% dos entrevistados consideravam o imunizante seguro para crianças. Em 2026, esse percentual caiu para 76%.

Para Renato Kfouri, a desinformação é o principal fator para esse cenário, mas não é o único obstáculo à imunização.

O infectologista menciona dificuldades de acesso aos serviços de saúde, horários de funcionamento dos postos de vacinação e, principalmente, a redução da percepção sobre a gravidade do sarampo.

Com a doença controlada durante anos em diversos países, parte da população deixou de conhecer diretamente suas consequências.

"É fundamental que a nossa geração, que não viveu esse período de circulação, que não conhece a doença, saiba disso. Isso vale também para os profissionais da saúde", afirma Kfouri.

O especialista destaca que lembrar a gravidade do sarampo é essencial para aumentar a adesão à vacinação.

Sarampo pode causar pneumonia, inflamação no cérebro e morte

Embora muitas vezes seja associado apenas a manchas vermelhas na pele, o sarampo pode provocar complicações graves e até levar à morte.

Entre os grupos mais vulneráveis estão crianças pequenas, especialmente menores de um ano, e pessoas imunossuprimidas.

De acordo com informações do Ministério da Saúde, as principais complicações incluem pneumonia, otite média aguda e encefalite.

Pneumonia: ocorre em aproximadamente uma a cada 20 crianças com sarampo e é a causa mais comum de morte pela doença entre crianças pequenas.

Otite média aguda: atinge cerca de uma a cada 10 crianças e pode provocar perda auditiva permanente.

Encefalite: inflamação no cérebro que pode ocorrer em uma a quatro de cada mil crianças infectadas. Aproximadamente 10% das crianças que desenvolvem essa complicação podem morrer.

Morte: entre uma e três de cada mil crianças com sarampo podem morrer em decorrência das complicações.

Além dos problemas durante a infecção, a doença também pode comprometer temporariamente as defesas do organismo.

Esse fenômeno é conhecido como amnésia imunológica.

"O sarampo deixa o que nós chamamos de uma amnésia imunológica, ou seja, durante três a seis meses até, você vê os indivíduos que foram acometidos pelo sarampo mais vulneráveis a internações, a hospitalizações, a outras infecções", explica Kfouri.

Isso significa que, mesmo depois da recuperação dos sintomas iniciais, a pessoa pode permanecer mais vulnerável a outras doenças infecciosas.

O especialista lembra que o sarampo já foi responsável por grande número de hospitalizações e mortes, principalmente entre crianças, antes da ampla utilização das vacinas.

Os primeiros sinais podem ser confundidos com os de outras infecções virais.

Entre os sintomas mais comuns estão febre alta, geralmente acima de 38,5°C, tosse seca, conjuntivite e mal-estar intenso.

As manchas vermelhas características da doença costumam aparecer entre três e cinco dias após o início dos sintomas.

Inicialmente, surgem no rosto e atrás das orelhas e, depois, espalham-se pelo restante do corpo.

Segundo Kfouri, a evolução da doença geralmente ocorre ao longo de aproximadamente uma semana, mas alguns pacientes podem apresentar complicações.

A persistência da febre depois do surgimento das manchas é considerada um sinal de alerta, especialmente em crianças menores de cinco anos.

A orientação do Ministério da Saúde é procurar atendimento médico diante de sintomas suspeitos.

Quem deve tomar a vacina contra o sarampo?

A principal forma de prevenção é a vacinação com a tríplice viral, que protege contra sarampo, caxumba e rubéola.

Segundo o Ministério da Saúde, o Calendário Nacional de Vacinação estabelece a aplicação de duas doses na infância:

Aos 12 meses: primeira dose da tríplice viral.

Aos 15 meses: segunda dose para completar o esquema previsto na infância.

Dos 5 aos 29 anos: pessoas não vacinadas ou com esquema incompleto devem ter pelo menos duas doses documentadas.

Dos 30 aos 59 anos: a recomendação de rotina é de pelo menos uma dose.

Em situações específicas, como surtos, o Ministério da Saúde pode ampliar a vacinação para outros grupos.

Em agosto, por exemplo, a pasta ampliou a recomendação de vacinação contra o sarampo em São Paulo para pessoas de seis meses a 59 anos, conforme as estratégias de controle da doença.

Kfouri ressalta que pessoas com duas doses documentadas, quando esse é o esquema indicado, não precisam receber uma terceira dose de rotina.

A proteção oferecida pela vacina é elevada. Segundo os dados apresentados, duas doses da tríplice viral têm eficácia de aproximadamente 97% na prevenção da infecção.

"Quanto mais vacinados nós tivermos, eles acabam funcionando como barreira e impedindo a disseminação do vírus. Sem organismos suscetíveis à infecção, as cadeias de transmissão vão se encerrando", afirma Kfouri.

articles.title: At 60, French artist Robert Tatin began a 21-year sculptural project around his home, filling the grounds with towering painted-cement figures, gates and gardens
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable journey of French artist Robert Tatin, who at 60 years old, transformed his hamlet in Mayenne into a mesmerizing sculpture garden over 21 years, showcasing towering figures and painted cement works. Learn about Tatin's legacy and the ongoing evolution of the Musée Robert Tatin.
articles.body: Most artists have a peaceful studio ahead of them and a lifetime of work behind them when they reach 60. French painter and ceramicist Robert Tatin decided to start the largest undertaking of his life at that very moment. He moved to La Frénouse, a small hamlet in the Mayenne area of western France, close to the town of Cossé-le-Vivien in 1962. Over the course of the following 21 years, he covered the grounds surrounding his home with imposing painted cement figures, gates, and gardens. The outcome is what tourists today refer to as the Musée Robert Tatin, one of France's most peculiar art places.The Musée Robert Tatin itself informs us that at the age of 60, Tatin conceived and launched a gigantic sculptural project surrounding his dwelling. He drew on his experience with the builders of Brasília and technical developments in reinforced cement mortar to produce what the museum calls an arch sculpture, built over 21 years from several ideas and drawings.A life before the gardenTatin was born in 1902 and originally became renowned as a ceramist; it was modelling clay that gained him his early recognition. He had come to art via painting and had travelled much. The museum’s biography says Tatin left France for South America in 1950 and returned in 1955. He spent several years on the French Riviera before settling permanently in Mayenne in 1962, where he began developing the monumental sculpture garden. In France he perceived the landscape in front of his villa at Mayenne as a sort of promised land.He wasn’t a lone wolf. His wife Lise was heavily involved in the building, and the museum says that the couple had a sewing workshop on the first floor of the house from 1968 until 1976. Tatin aspired to build a global language, a bridge between East and West, and soon the first painted cement sculptures appeared in what he dubbed the Garden of Meditations.Giants, gates and a gardenTatin created the Allée des Géants as the approach to the site, lining an avenue almost 80 metres long with 19 monumental painted-cement statues. The figures represent people from his artistic and historical imagination, from Joan of Arc to Alfred Jarry. On the museum’s façade, the Gate of the Giants displays large high-relief portraits of artists he admired, including Rembrandt, Van Gogh, Leonardo da Vinci, Goya and Delacroix. Raw Vision and SPACES document these features as part of the site’s design.Beyond the avenue is the Garden of Meditations, some 500 square metres in area. It goes from the Sun Gate (representing the sunrise) to the Moon Gate (representing the sunset). In the centre is a 6.5 metre statue of the Lady of All the World, and structures representing the twelve months around a small pond. Rooms off the garden show Tatin’s paintings, ceramics and lithographs.The complete site has often been compared with the Ideal Palace erected by postman Ferdinand Cheval in the Drôme, and the resemblance is appropriate. Both were the work of one determined man, built over many years out of whatever materials and with whatever techniques were at hand. By the time Tatin died in 1983, he had spent more than two decades shaping the site into a distinctive art environment.A museum that keeps growingThe museum’s history records that after Tatin’s death in 1983, the property passed into public hands. It became an official Musée de France in 2002, and in 2012 the house where Robert and Lise lived received the Maison des Illustres label from France’s Ministry of Culture. The original sculptural ensemble is considered complete, while the wider museum experience continues to develop through temporary exhibitions in La Grange and contemporary sculptures displayed across its five hectares of gardens.The residential and sculptural elements reflect Tatin’s vision of a village of living, moving artisans. His legacy is a reminder that ambition need not end at 60 years of age. Tatin started late, laboured for more than twenty years and developed a destination that still draws visitors in a secluded part of Mayenne.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 1964, a California sculptor began a 150-foot steel-and-concrete dinosaur to lure drivers to his diner; building it took 11 years and $250,000
articles.summary: Discover the story of how Claude Bell constructed a 150-foot dinosaur in California to attract diners, turning it into a beloved landmark. Learn about its history, materials, and transformations through the years.
articles.body: In 1964, Claude Bell, former Knott’s Berry Farm sculptor, began constructing a giant dinosaur beside Interstate 10 in Cabazon, California. He hoped to attract motorists to his Wheel Inn restaurant, and the result was a 150-foot-long, 45-foot-high structure called Dinny. According to the Los Angeles Times, it took Bell 11 years and $250,000 to complete the construction, made from salvaged steel and concrete from nearby construction. What was initially an advertising idea became a landmark motorists travelling through Southern California recognised.How Bell turned salvaged materials into a roadside attractionThe project’s inspiration came from Bell’s childhood when he visited Atlantic City in 1906 and saw a local landmark there: an elephant-shaped building called Lucy. The experience stimulated his ambition to create a roadside structure that was equally distinctive. Dinny was made using a steel framework to support its structure, which was reinforced with rods and heavy girders.The girders were sourced from a drive-in theatre that was no longer in use in Banning, while the rest of the materials were recovered from nearby Interstate 10 construction. After it was cross-braced and welded, the framework was covered with approximately 1,200 bags of cement. The dinosaur’s exterior was shaped by Bell himself; he ran his gloved hands over cement to achieve a textured skin and chose a greenish-brown finish because the dinosaur’s actual colours were unknown. The finished structure worked as both a giant roadside advertisement and a building with functional indoor space.A doorway in the tail of Dinny leads to an 18-by-56-foot main room, while the dinosaur housed another apartment in its back. Initially, Bell’s idea was to use the main room as a restaurant or cocktail lounge, but he quit on it because he wanted visitors to be curious when they entered and explored the structure. Eventually, the interior ended up accommodating a museum.Another giant dinosaur was in the cards for Bell, a Tyrannosaurus rex called Mr Rex, whose construction began in 1981 and was supposed to be 65 feet in height. The original plans included a winding staircase towards its mouth, which visitors were supposed to climb and, through its teeth, look across the desert. Bell’s other ambition extended beyond the two dinosaurs, and it included adding a woolly mammoth and smaller prehistoric animals to create a dinosaur garden, but those additions never materialised.From the Wheel Inn to a Hollywood landmarkAfter Bell passed away in 1988, the property underwent a new phase after a development company took over the site and expanded its attractions, ABC 10 reported. The additions saw the development of robotic dinosaurs, a dinosaur bone pit, and a gift shop inside Dinny. The property was also given a new look as a visitor destination rather than serving its original role as a roadside attraction to entice customers to the Wheel Inn. Hollywood also helped put the dinosaurs on the map with elevated status after they appeared in Pee-wee's Big Adventure and The Wizard. Moreover, the way the Dinosaurs’ interior was used also went through major changes; SPACES Archives records show that Dinny’s interior became a museum dedicated to Young Earth Creationism.As of today, the Cabazon Dinosaurs stand at 50770 Seminole Drive in Cabazon, California, where visitors can explore dinosaur displays and other attractions. Although Bell never finished his planned prehistoric garden and the Wheel Inn was demolished in 2016, Dinny and Mr. Rex remain roadside landmarks, outlasting the restaurant they were built to promote.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hospitals ‘overcharging’ is a malpractice: Govt to Supreme Court
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Govt has admitted before Supreme Court the “malpractice” of hospitals charging patients high MRPs for medicines and consumables, and said it
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Govt has admitted before Supreme Court the “malpractice” of hospitals charging patients high MRPs for medicines and consumables, and said it was conscious of the problem, examining it and devising appropriate interventions in consultation with all stakeholders.In an affidavit filed in SC on the issue of capping prices of all medicines and medical consumables, chemicals and fertilisers ministry said that patients have a very low bargaining position with respect to hospitals, resulting in various malpractices. The affidavit noted the irony of India being home to companies making cheap drugs but patients here having to pay way above the manufacturing price, as well as patients being subjected to overcharging by hospitals.“The Indian drug market is fairly competitive, with a large number of pharmaceutical companies in every drug segment, resulting in one of the lowest prices in the world. Ordinarily, where there is substantial competition, there is no need to regulate prices. However, by their very nature, health treatment and pharmaceutical products involve information and bargaining asymmetries between patients on the one hand, and retail pharmacies, hospital pharmacies, hospitals providing treatment and doctors on the other,” the affidavit said.Hospitals charge up to 700% premium on cancer drugsThe govt affidavit said a patient has a “very low bargaining position vis-a-vis the hospital, and the patient’s knowledge of drugs, their substitutes and their prices is also very limited”. These bargaining and information asymmetries result in various malpractices in the system despite strong competition among manufacturers, leading to the need for regulation, it said.Enumerating the steps taken by it to control the pricing of drugs, govt said ceiling prices for 935 scheduled formulations and retail prices of 3,881 new drugs have been fixed. Govt filed the affidavit on a plea filed by Dr Sanjay Kulshrestha, who referred to a Niti Aayog report and a 2020 statement of the then health minister Harsh Vardhan that expenditure on health pushed an estimated six crore families below the poverty line each year.The affidavit said hospitals buy medicines from manufacturers who provide highest trade margin and then sell those medicines to patients at MRP, with margins ranging from 170% to 700% or more in the case of anti-cancer drugs.“That another area of concern in the sector is the supply of consumables in hospitals, where margins of 100% to 1000% or more are prevalent, along with a tendency of hospitals to purchase consumables that have a high MRP and margin, with a low price to the distributor/hospital. Ordinarily, hospital supplies are included in the package cost for treatment of major diseases/procedures under govt schemes/insurance, and govt/insurance agencies negotiate and fix the lowest rate for such packages. However, for patients making direct payment to the hospital, hospital supplies are billed separately at MRP,” it said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A 160-year-old New York tradition is headed for extinction
articles.summary: New York City lawmakers approved a ban on horse-drawn carriages that will phase out the historic tradition by June 2028.
articles.body:
A New York tradition more than a century old is ending.

The New York City Council on Oct. 22 voted to ban horse-drawn carriages , winding down a historic tradition that's popular among tourists and fiercely opposed by animal rights groups.

In a majority vote, the 51-member council approved a ban prohibiting new carriage licenses and the ending the operation of horse carriages by June 2028.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani supports the bill and is expected to sign it into law. In early October, he declared that the horse carriage industry is "coming to an end in New York City."

The city's horse carriages have traversed a loop in Central Park dating back to the 1800s. By the mid-20th century, the city limited horse-drawn carriage licenses to 68. Over the decades, the carriages became a tourism staple and appeared in iconic films and television shows, such as "Sex and the City," "Elf" and "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York."

But in recent years, animal rights groups and others have increasingly called for the end to the tradition, arguing that the practice subjects horses to harsh unnatural conditions and physical exhaustion.

Opposition mounted this summer after the death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan , an Indian tourist killed in June after being thrown from a horse carriage. The legislation phasing out the longstanding tradition is named after Mahajan.

The same month, a horse named Deniz had collapsed suddenly in Central Park while pulling a carriage with passengers, setting off another wave of backlash against the horse-carriage industry.

President Donald Trump , who is from New York, called horse carriages a "great tradition" and said they "will be missed."

"The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience. So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!" he said in a post on Truth Social .

Some who oppose the legislation say it does not adequately protect workers who rely on the carriages for their income. Officials say there are about 150 horse-carriage drivers currently working in the city.

"If the NYC Council bans horse-carriage rides, hundreds of blue-collar drivers, owners, and their family members will be financially ruined and emotionally devastated," the Transport Workers Union of America said in a statement on X.

Protesters rally outside City Hall over horse-carriage ban proposal

Joann Ariola, a councilmember representing a portion of Queens, removed her name as a sponsor for the ban the day before the city council approved it, writing in a statement that carriage drivers deserve "a clear path forward before their ability to earn a living is taken away."

The bill requires the mayor's office to develop a transition plan by April 2027 and to consider a program to compensate carriage operators for their businesses and help with the disposition of their horses. Under the proposal, the horses could not be slaughtered.

City Hall has promised that it is working toward a transition to help protect carriage workers.

"We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all," City Hall spokesperson Sneha Choudhary previously told USA TODAY.

New York City is the latest major metropolitan area that's voted to ban horse-drawn carriages. Over the last five years, cities including Philadelphia, Chicago and San Antonio have outlawed the practice.

Christopher Cann is a national reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him by email at ccann@usatoday.com .

articles.title: Will back all meaningful efforts for Ukraine peace, PM Modi assures Poland's Tusk
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Looking to further expand their strategic partnership, India and Poland agreed to double bilateral trade by 2030 and announced dialogue
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Looking to further expand their strategic partnership, India and Poland agreed to double bilateral trade by 2030 and announced dialogue mechanisms for defence industrial collaboration and counterterrorism cooperation as PM Narendra Modi hosted his counterpart Donald Tusk for talks Thursday.Modi and Tusk expressed deepest concern in a joint statement over the war in Ukraine, including its tragic humanitarian consequences and the impact on Global South. In his media statement, Modi assured Tusk that whether it is Ukraine or West Asia, India will continue to support every meaningful effort for peace.Poland views the war in Ukraine as a direct threat to its national security and sovereignty due to its shared border, influx of refugees and the threat of future Russian aggression in eastern Europe.“They reiterated the need for a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in line with international law, consistent with the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, including respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity,” said the joint statement. The leaders also noted the negative impacts of the war on global food and energy security, especially for the Global South.Modi and Tusk, the first Polish PM to visit India in 16 years, also backed an MoU under negotiation for cooperation in critical minerals.Modi said the friendship between India and Poland was based not only on diplomatic ties but also on a shared heritage of humanity and empathy. He recalled how, during the Second World War, the royal families of Jamnagar and Kolhapur had provided shelter in India to thousands of Polish children and families. He also thanked Poland for helping India evacuate Indian students from Ukraine shortly after the Russia-Ukraine war began in 2022.Modi said the world was passing through a period of uncertainty and change, and even in such times, both India and Poland were emerging as important hubs of growth, technology and innovation.“Today we have agreed to deepen ties in defence, space and nuclear energy. In all these strategic sectors, we invite Polish companies to engage in co-development and co-production with India,” he said.He also announced a startup bridge to facilitate cooperation in IT, Artificial Intelligence and critical technologies.“Both India and Poland believe in democratic values and the rule of law,” Modi said, underlining that both sides considered reforms essential to make global governance institutions more empowered.The two countries agreed that the UN needed structural reforms, including expansion of UNSC in both permanent and non-permanent categories, to remain relevant, credible and effective. In the joint statement, Poland expressed support for India’s membership of a more inclusive, reformed and expanded UNSC, as well as its candidature for a non-permanent seat on the council for 2028-29.Modi and Tusk unequivocally condemned terrorism, including cross-border terrorism, and stressed that there could be no justification for terrorism on any grounds.“They condemned in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in J&K’s Pahalgam on 22 April, 2025. They called for strong and concerted action against terrorists and terrorist entities, including those designated by the UNSC 1267 sanctions committee,” said the joint statement.Defence and security cooperation was a major focus, with the leaders underlining importance of an Agreement on Mutual Protection and Exchange of Classified Information and expressing expectation it would be signed soon.They proposed a defence industry dialogue to develop a “forward-looking framework for defence industrial cooperation”, including business-to-business engagement and, where mutually agreed, partnerships in technology, co-development, co-production and other forms of collaboration.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: UK to draft in military aircraft to fight wildfires, Burnham says
articles.summary: The prime minister is hosting the UK's first wildfire summit to prepare for future blazes after a record summer 2026.
articles.body:
Military planes and helicopters will be drafted in to tackle wildfires, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to tell the UK's first summit on the issue.

Civilian fire services in all four nations will be able to request the support of the Royal Air Force's Chinook helicopters and A400M planes to fight wildfires on tough terrain such as remote moorland and steep hillsides.

Burnham said the measures were needed because "we cannot put people through another summer like this one".

The government will host its first "wildfire resilience summit" on Friday to discuss how to prevent, respond to and recover from such blazes after a record-breaking summer 2026.

There have been 1,350 wildfires in England and Wales this year, an all-time high and up by more than 300 on last year and more than 1,000 on 2024, according to figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council .

Records for the number of reported wildfires were also broken in 2022 and 2025 - but the UK's Climate Change Committee has warned the risk will rise in the coming decades.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said this was the first time the RAF's Chinooks and the four-engine A400Ms were being equipped to tackle wildfires. Some areas struggled with no air assistance in the summer.

RAF Chinook crews have already helped respond to wildfires in Cyprus.

In addition to military aircraft, the government said it would also spend £45m on wildfire-specific personal protective equipment for firefighters on the ground.

It is lighter than current firefighting equipment which is designed for fires in buildings and not meant to be worn for a long time, the government added.

Ministers are also pledging a £25m scheme from April 2027 to April 2029 to restore dried-out peatlands in England so they are natural firebreaks, and financial support for farmers to fireproof their land such as by digging ponds.

"The government will also look at tougher local restrictions or product bans to stop people starting fires when the risk is high," a briefing ahead of the summit said, following a temporary ban on disposable BBQs .

Burnham will meet fire chiefs, local leaders and experts from tech companies at the summit.

"I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything," he said on Thursday, recounting the night of a wildfire that destroyed 19 homes in the West Midlands in August.

"I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn't have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs."

Earlier this month, MPs on the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee said there were weaknesses in the UK's wildfire preparedness , including access to aerial firefighting resources, securing water supplies during major incidents and coordinating resources at a national level.

MPs said the current system for obtaining aerial firefighting support was "no longer fit for purpose".

At the summit, a "Wildfires AI Unit" will be announced to combine universities, tech firms and officials on the Cobra emergency committee, along with Met Office wildfire forecasts and closer work with devolved governments.

In August, the government convened a Cobra meeting before sending an emergency alert to millions of phones across England and Wales - which sparked a backlash from some .

Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record, according to the Met Office. In a study on how this summer was impacted by human-induced climate change, it said the heat experienced was made 130 times more likely .

"The wildfires that tore through our countryside this summer showed the urgent need to adapt to our changing climate," Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said ahead of the summit.

"Nature is our greatest ally in preventing wildfires starting in the first place," she added.

Major incidents were declared for wildfires this year in areas such as Dunwich Heath and RSPB Minsmere in Suffolk, the Cairngorms , Hampshire and Holme Fen in Cambridgeshire.

articles.title: A necklace nearly taken to a car boot sale with a £15 price tag was later identified as a rare South Pacific treasure; expected to fetch just £60 to £100, it sold for £99,000 at auction
articles.summary: A necklace nearly taken to a car boot sale with a £15 price tag turned out to be a rare 18th-century Polynesian treasure worth almost £100,000.
articles.body: A necklace nearly taken to a car boot sale with a £15 price tag turned out to be a rare 18th-century Polynesian treasure worth almost £100,000. The piece, made from human hair and sperm whale bone and originating from the Austral Islands in the South Pacific, had been found during a house clearance. At Ewbank’s auctioneers in Surrey, it sold for £99,000, far above its original estimate of £60 to £100, according to Antique Collecting and the Antiques Trade Gazette.Nearly lost at a car boot saleThe necklace was brought to Ewbank’s by the owner of a house clearance firm, who had no idea of its significance. It was part of a batch of items that had been priced at £15 and was destined for the A3 car boot sale opposite the auction rooms. At the last moment, the owner changed his mind and took the necklace to Ewbank’s instead. That decision transformed the fate of an object that might otherwise have been sold for a few pounds at a roadside stall, as per the reports.The auction house identified it as a rare late 18th-century necklace from the Austral Islands. Made from hair and sperm whale bone, it belonged to a category of Polynesian material culture that is highly prized by collectors and museums.Why the necklace was valuableThe necklace’s value came from its age, rarity and cultural importance. Objects made from human hair and whale bone were significant in Polynesian societies, and surviving examples from the late 1700s are exceptionally scarce. Ewbank’s senior partner and auctioneer Chris Ewbank said, according to Antique Collecting Magazine, that the piece was a rare late 18th-century necklace emanating from the Austral Islands. Its materials and provenance placed it firmly within the field of tribal art, where authenticity and historical context can dramatically affect value.Before the sale, interest from collectors suggested the necklace might reach £20,000 to £30,000. Even that estimate was hundreds of times higher than the £15 price originally attached to it, as per the report.A dramatic bidding battleThe final sale exceeded every expectation. A bidder in the auction room dropped out at £50,000, leaving a French bidder using Ewbank’s live online bidding platform to compete against an Australian telephone bidder. The contest pushed the hammer price to £99,000, as per the reports. It became the highest sale at Ewbank’s in 2016 and the highest price achieved on the firm’s live bidding platform, which had been launched earlier that year.The result showed how competitive the market for rare tribal art can be. Collectors were not simply buying an old necklace, but a rare surviving object connected to the material traditions of the South Pacific.From £15 to £99,000The story is remarkable because of the enormous gap between the necklace’s initial valuation and its final sale price. A £15 item became a £99,000 auction result, a rise of more than 6,000 times its original price.It also illustrates the importance of expert assessment. Many valuable antiques are overlooked because they look worn, unusual or unfamiliar, particularly when they do not resemble conventional European jewellery or furniture.For collectors, the case is a reminder that provenance, materials and age can matter more than immediate appearance. A small object from a house clearance can carry a history that only specialist knowledge can reveal.A lesson for anyone clearing a homeHouse clearances often uncover objects that owners no longer recognise or understand. While most items will not turn out to be rare Polynesian artefacts, the necklace shows why it can be worth having unusual pieces examined before they are sold cheaply.Old jewellery, carvings, textiles, weapons, shells and bone objects can all fall into specialist categories. Auction houses, museums and tribal art experts can help identify whether an item has historical or cultural significance.In this case, one last-minute decision saved a rare South Pacific necklace from a car boot sale and brought it before collectors who understood its true importance. The £99,000 result was not just a windfall, but proof that overlooked objects can still hold extraordinary stories.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: Miley Cyrus recently stepped up to help a fan during an emotional battle with breast cancer. The singer met with Cash Jacobs, a fellow musician, after one of her shows at the Hollywood Bowl earlier this month. During their hang, Cyrus helped Jacobs, who has Stage 3 breast cancer, shave her head in preparation for her chemotherapy treatments. The process was captured in a video that was shared on social media Oct. 21. And for Jacobs, the moment was profoundly meaningful. “thank you @miley. For making me feel safe and comfortable, for giving me your time, and for being exactly who you are,” Jacobs wrote in the post’s caption. “It is a huge gift to continue to watch you grow and you are forever my biggest inspiration. Stay soft and strong 🤍” In the video, Cyrus gives Jacobs some uplifting advice. The “Flowers” star also says a few words before the makeover. “Thank you to the universe for bringing us together, and celebrating our connection and what music does for the world — it brings people like you and me together that may never meet,” Cyrus says. The video then gets into the makeover process. “Let’s go girl,” Cyrus says, before taking the buzzers to Jacobs’ head. The pair share some light moments as well, with Cyrus remarking on how great Jacobs looks in the new ‘do. “You got cute ears, you got a good-shaped head, you got a gorg face,” Cyrus says. Jacobs initially got connected with Cyrus after she posted a video, sharing her breast cancer journey and calling on the singer to be the one to shave her head. The internet responded by tagging Cyrus and ultimately, the “Malibu” songstress came through. In her Oct. 21 post, Jacobs explained that Cyrus not only flew her out to Los Angeles and gave her tickets to the show, but also helped her through “one of the scariest and most intimate moments of my life.” “They say don’t meet your idols. Well I did. And it was everything and more,” Jacobs wrote. She added that Cyrus’ music has always uplifted her during difficult moments in her life. “And when they pass, I can listen to her songs and be reminded that I got through it and came out stronger,” Jacobs wrote. “Between major depressive episodes and finding out I have stage 3 breast cancer. I am lucky enough to have reached her and her team and been given this opportunity of a lifetime.” Jacobs also thanked the internet for making it all happen, before praising Cyrus for her kindness. “Miley is the softest, coolest, KINDEST, and most genuine human being I’ve ever had the privilege of meeting and spending time with. And not to mention her SHAVING MY F***ING HEAD!!!!! WHAT?!?” Jacobs wrote. “I want to hold on to this moment and to always remember the conversations we had and what they mean for me.” Cyrus’ two nights at the Hollywood Bowl have been all-around emotional. The singer, whose recent performances marked her first solo shows since 2022, broke down as she paid tribute to her godmother, the late country legend Dolly Parton, on opening night. “Me and Dolly, we are eternal,” Cyrus said, speaking to the crowd as she sat at the edge of the stage. “Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart.”

articles.title: US-sanctioned ICC wins Sakharov Prize, EU’s top human rights award
articles.summary: The prize comes less than two weeks after US President Donald Trump announced sanctions against the court.
articles.body:
The European Union has awarded the International Criminal Court (ICC) its top human rights award, two weeks after US President Donald Trump vowed to dismantle the court through new sanctions .

Thursday’s Sakharov Prize is the second international recognition for the war crimes tribunal this month, with former ICC Judge Navi Pillay awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her work to promote peace and international law.

“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” said European Parliament President Roberta Metsola in announcing the award.

The ICC thanked the European Parliament for the honour “at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges”.

“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said.

The Hague-based ICC has long been a target of Trump, whose campaign against it has escalated since the court announced in 2024 arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant.

The Trump administration has promised to dismantle the court “brick by brick”, recently announcing sanctions aimed at crippling its day-to-day operations. The ICC tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a video posted on social media when the sanctions were announced.

Washington has also sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, as well as a UN special rapporteur focusing on the occupied Palestinian territories and Palestinian rights groups that have provided evidence to the court.

The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the US sanctions, which are due to come into force in six months, and has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to make sure the court can continue functioning.

“The International Criminal Court must be free to pursue its mission, independently, and without pressure or intimidation,” EU chief Ursula von der Leyen posted online after the prize was announced.

Brussels is hoping to use the delay before the sanctions are applied to try to talk the US down, but according to EU officials is also eyeing implementing a “blocking statute” to shield the ICC from Washington.

articles.body: A house that began as a modest ranch in 1958 has evolved into one of the more unusual residential properties in Goose Creek, South Carolina. Featuring three kitchens, themed bedrooms and an expansive indoor swimming pool, the 5,390-square-foot estate is now on the market for $1.227 million. According to Realtor dot com, which featured the property in a report by Tiffani Sherman published on October 20, 2026, the home has retained much of its distinctive character over the years. Property listings published by local real estate firms, including Beresford Realty’s listing through Seignious & Smith, confirm its size, asking price and unusual layout. Located at 108 Hampton Avenue, the property occupies 1.21 acres in the former Oaks Country Club community. Its combination of midcentury architecture, eclectic interiors and resort-style amenities sets it apart from the newer residential developments emerging in the surrounding area.A house with three kitchens and distinct personalitiesThe residence has four bedrooms, four full bathrooms and two half-bathrooms, according to the property listing. Three kitchens are distributed across its living spaces, including a compact bistro-style kitchen serving the upstairs primary suite. The arrangement creates possibilities beyond those of a conventional single-family home. Separate entrances and self-contained living areas could make the property suitable for multigenerational households or potentially multiple short-term rental units, subject to applicable approvals.The interiors reflect the original owners’ eclectic tastes. One bedroom features an African-inspired theme, while another draws on Victorian aesthetics. Decorative details, varied materials and individual room designs give the house a character that differs from the uniformity of many contemporary developments. The current owner purchased the property in 2023 and largely preserved its existing furnishings and décor, according to Realtor dot com. Rather than undertaking a comprehensive modernisation, the owner retained much of the home’s established look.An indoor pool beneath soaring ceilingsThe standout feature is a two-storey, enclosed indoor pool and recreation area measuring approximately 2,423 square feet. Its ceilings rise 31 feet, creating a dramatic space that functions as more than a swimming area. The recreational zone includes room for a pool table, darts and exercise equipment, alongside features such as a swing and slide. A nearby living area and bedroom further integrate the pool complex into the house’s overall layout. The property also has substantial outdoor space, mature trees and brick fencing, with additional structures including a storage shed and a covered, three-bay area. The listing describes the grounds as offering room for outdoor activities and gatherings.A property with multiple possibilitiesBeyond its unusual interiors, the estate offers potential flexibility for a buyer willing to work with its existing layout. The land originally comprised three lots, and the listing indicates that subdivision may be possible, subject to county requirements and approvals.The property is also advertised as a licensed short-term rental, although prospective buyers would need to verify the licence conditions and any restrictions that apply to future use. Some major systems have reportedly received more recent attention, including the roof, pool pump and three HVAC systems. However, the house is being sold largely as is, leaving buyers to decide whether to preserve its existing interiors or introduce their own updates.With its expansive pool room, multiple kitchens and highly individualised décor, the Goose Creek property offers an alternative to the conventional luxury home. Its asking price of $1.227 million reflects not only its size and location but also the unusual combination of features that has made it a distinctive listing in the Charleston-area housing market.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Traitor behaviour splits opinion as paranoia deepens
articles.summary: The murder in plain sight victim was revealed ahead of another difficult round table.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode seven of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Six days is a long time in The Celebrity Traitors.

So it was a relief to be put out of our misery as last Friday's literal yawn-fest came to its slow-burning conclusion; the traitorous trio eventually succeeding in their mission to kill in plain sight.

The snoozefest - which involved reluctant traitor James Acaster making faithful Ross Kemp yawn by boring him to tears - meant the paranoid EastEnders star was finally put out of his misery.

On learning his fate, the actor turned to Shakespeare - who else?

"To thine own self be true," he declared, quoting Polonius from Hamlet.

As usual at breakfast, the faithfuls seated early mused over who may have been murdered overnight: "If Jerry's not here, I don't think I can handle it," Romesh Ranganathan confessed.

Jerry Hall was charmingly late to the party. After everyone had discussed Ross's demise, she piped up in her famous Texan drawl: "Is Ross gone?"

As the typical off-the-wall theories began to swirl, Jerry later told Miranda Hart she suspected fellow faithful James Blunt - for the very plausible reason that "his face is redder than a fox's ass at gooseberry time". It's as good a reason as any proffered so far this series.

Once the croissant crumbs had been cleared, it was time for a mission that threw the cat among the pigeons - not least because the traitor's lair it took place in "smelled like a litter tray", according to Jerry.

Miranda felt there were more complex olfactory notes at play: "A mix of salmon, cheap cologne and crotch." Delightful.

The mission involved each player having to build a shield on a plinth in front of them out of 3D jigsaw-type pieces which were buried in troughs in sawdust. Think Krypton Factor meets lucky dip.

At three intervals, a bell would ring, and the players all had to stop and put on blindfolds for a few minutes. The traitors could then remove theirs and go about sabotaging the handiwork of anyone they fancied.

And while James A revealed he was "starting to have more fun" after murdering poor Ross, if there was a prize for the worst traitor of all time, he would still smash it.

He was too scared to take off his blindfold and remove any shield pieces from the faithfuls, leaving the dirty work - and all the risk - to fellow traitors Maya Jama and King Kenny. Suffice to say, they were not impressed.

"He didn't even lift the blindfold off - I'm speechless," said Maya.

James A knew he was in trouble: "I'm aware I'll get a dressing down in the turret but I am the one who killed Grant Mitchell."

He wasn't wrong about the telling off. And the fact he completed his own puzzle, earning himself a shield, must have really riled his co-conspirators.

To be fair, you could argue he's playing a blinder - there's been very little suspicion of him so far.

Three other celebrities also managed to complete their shield puzzles - James B, Joanne McNall and Michael Sheen - but no money was banked after Maya and Kenny panicked and didn't remove any pieces at their last opportunity.

But the task at least threw up another bunch of mad theories for the faithfuls to chew over, as they tried to unsuccessfully guess where the floorboard creaking was coming from as two of the traitors tried to creep around the room.

It was good news for Romesh at least, whose hay fever saved the day - Sharon Rooney could hear him sniffing constantly next to her so knew he couldn't have been a traitor.

Maybe the tickly moustache isn't helping his allergies - and combing it won't make much difference.

Ahead of the round table, self-styled "Poundland Poirot" Sharon was living up to her nickname with a red herring theory about a perfume bottle being used to kill someone in plain sight.

Ross's murder and the disorienting mission ultimately confused everyone, with the round table being the most random of the series so far.

Leigh-Ann Pinnock, Bash Croft, Joanne and Jerry were among the accused, with Jerry - having survived murder overnight - banished for being "a professional pot stirrer. She's "planted more seeds than a farmer's market" – or at least that was Joanne's reasoning.

Romesh's deadpan excuse was better: "I've long suspected she preferred Rob (his comedy partner and former contestant Rob Beckett) to me."

Once again, the faithfuls were left to rue losing one of their own, with Jerry chastising them as she made her grand exit: "I told you so!"

Leigh-Ann still had heat on her after Jerry's banishment, with her bright red - blood red? - leather-look long gloves drawing attention in the kitchen.

"I said they looked traitorous and villainous," she bemoaned.

Back in the turret, as James A predicted, Maya and Kenny were not happy about his lack of action at the mission.

"You hung us out to dry!" Maya chastised him.

But he redeemed himself somewhat by declaring that he had finally got a taste for villainy.

"When I killed Ross Kemp in plain sight, I loved it!" James A told a delighted Maya and Kenny.

It's only taken him three-quarters of the series to get there but better late than never.

articles.title: Grid operator says lights will stay on this winter after concerns
articles.summary: The assurance from the National Energy System Operator comes amid concern from its engineers about their ability to ensure adequate supply.
articles.body:
The body in charge of Britain's electricity network has given assurances that the lights will stay on this winter after concerns were raised by some of its engineers.

The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months.

However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation.

NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days".

It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine.

"While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO.

In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables.

The release of the two reports comes as Britain's energy generation and security falls under increasing scrutiny, given the wars in the Middle East and eastern Europe have pushed prices up and sparked supply fears.

The country's electricity is generated from a wide range of sources, including renewables such as solar and wind, as well as more traditional gas-fired and nuclear power stations.

Wind power was the largest generator of electricity in Britain last year, accounting for almost 30% of all power, marginally above gas.

However, there appear to be challenges in the transition to renewables in ensuring supply keeps up with demand, according to findings from an investigation into practices at NESO, which was commissioned following allegations over operational decision making and record keeping at the grid operator.

Law firm Eversheds Sutherland, which carried out the independent investigation, said there were "high levels of stress and concern" within NESO's Electricity National Control Centre over the "current state of the energy industry generally" and the longer-term ability to keep it balanced.

It said this was, according to evidence gathered from staff, due to the fact that traditional methods of electricity generation such as gas were "easier to manage", compared to renewables, which were "less flexible", and were making the job of ensuring supply meets demand "more difficult".

The probe also found there to be a "significant disconnect" between those working in the control room and NESO's leadership.

Multiple witnesses expressed the view that those in senior leadership and executive positions "do not fully appreciate or understand either the way in which the control room works, or the reality of the pressures faced by those on the frontline who are responsible for 'keeping the lights on'", Eversheds' report said.

The investigation was prompted after Conservative shadow energy secretary Clare Coutinho said in July she had been contacted by a whistle-blower alleging that NESO had been "hiding information about how securely our grid is being run".

One of the claims was that control room staff were encouraged to conceal or alter records to avoid leaving a paper trail linked to efforts to stabilise the grid during a period of extreme heat in June.

This was done in order for NESO, which is owned by the government, to avoid public scrutiny or reputational damage, according to the allegation.

Eversheds said its investigation did not substantiate any of the allegations from whistle-blowers but did identify "cultural, governance and control issues" that it said were "significant findings in their own right".

Fintan Slye, chief executive of NESO, said the investigation identified "areas where we could improve how colleagues can raise concerns and how we respond to them".

"I want all colleagues at NESO to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make," he added.

articles.title: Surveillance and ‘constant paranoia’: Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
articles.summary: Officials compare working in Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine to the Cold War era.
articles.body:
"Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC.

US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War.

But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.

The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion.

They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts , and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials.

Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed.

Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia.

"There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty."

The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls.

Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater.

"Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow.

Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission.

The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution".

Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials.

One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy.

Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia

Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect

They fled Russia, but the West sent them back

Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police.

One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear.

Not everyone can deal with the pressure.

One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months.

'Generals prove what they can do in war. The same is true for diplomats'

In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre Lévy.

He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be.

The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible.

And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies.

Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country.

But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning.

After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Еven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers.

One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'."

Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses.

A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase.

"It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour."

Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage".

Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies.

This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs."

Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassador. "There are no calls, no meetings at ministerial level."

But they say this has made diplomats all the more important, left with the responsibility to communicate their governments' positions to Moscow.

"Generals prove what they can do during a war. The same is true for diplomats. When things get really difficult, every single thing you do actually matters."

Lynne Tracy left Moscow in 2025 feeling she had accomplished her primary mission: the US Embassy had held firm.

But she is also proud of the work she and her team did to maintain connection between Americans and ordinary Russians.

"Because at some point, government-to-government relations will have a chance to improve - and those ties between people will be there to help speed the improvement."

Russians turn to cash, putting more strain on slowing wartime economy

Threats, insults, and Kremlin 'robots': How Russian diplomacy died

articles.title: 'He put it back': Trump says Ukraine's Starlink access restored, stays silent on Musk
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has said Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's access to Starlink internet services after restrictions disrupted the connectivity
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has said Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's access to Starlink internet services after restrictions disrupted the connectivity used by Kyiv's military.However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the speed of the military's satellite internet connection had not yet returned to normal, suggesting that the restoration was still incomplete.Trump's comments came amid reports that he had personally contacted Musk, the owner of SpaceX, which operates Starlink, and asked him to lift the restrictions. Trump declined to confirm whether such a conversation had taken place but said, "Bottom line, he put it back."The Trump administration has previously denied ordering any restrictions on Ukraine's access to the service.Why Starlink matters to Ukraine's militaryUkraine depends heavily on Starlink for communications between military units, coordinating operations and receiving early warnings during Russian missile attacks.The satellite-based network also supports the use of drones, which Ukraine deploys both to strike Russian targets and to defend against incoming attacks. Disruptions to connectivity can therefore affect the military's ability to operate drones and respond to Russian assaults.The service at the centre of the dispute includes Starshield, a military-grade network provided through Musk's Starlink system. Ukraine uses Starshield for some military operations.Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon. His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had played a role in the restrictions. The White House has repeatedly denied instructing Musk's company to limit access.Zelenskyy says connection speed remains below normalSpeaking at a press conference on Thursday, Zelenskyy said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had not been fully restored."The speed has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet," he said, adding, "We are working on it."He also said he was awaiting information from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."The Ukrainian president spoke shortly before The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had called Musk to ask him to remove the restrictions. According to the newspaper, Trump was frustrated that Starlink speeds remained capped at around 160km/h.The report said the limits had reduced the effectiveness of Ukrainian offensive drones and interceptors against Russian attacks. Starlink appeared to be operating more normally on Thursday, shortly after the reported conversation between Trump and Musk.BBC News said it had not independently confirmed The Wall Street Journal's account and had contacted the White House and SpaceX for an explanation.Dispute comes amid wider pressure on KyivThe connectivity dispute comes as Trump increases pressure on Ukraine over its attacks on Russian oil refineries. The US president has argued that these strikes have contributed to rising oil prices.The administration has also waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed to a deal to import Russian diesel into the US market. These moves have drawn criticism from Ukraine and its European allies.Ukraine had reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October, adding to concerns about the support available to its armed forces.The latest developments highlight how access to satellite communications and intelligence can affect Ukraine's ability to sustain military operations as the war with Russia continues.You use AI every day. articles.title: Almost all shallow-water coral reefs now face extinction risk, study warns
articles.summary: World authority on threatened wildlife classifies 96 percent of assessed coral reef systems as “critically endangered”.
articles.body:
Almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse in the next 50 years, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) has warned in a new global assessment.

In a report released on Thursday, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of the planet’s coral reef systems as “critically endangered”, its highest risk category, with total extinction possible by 2075.

“The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems,” said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

Corals are heat-sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change , which is warming the world’s oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.

When a reef collapses, hard corals disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges. As a result, the reef no longer supports a diverse ecosystem that can include everything from tiny invertebrates to reef fish like grouper.

The emergence this year of a “super” El Nino, the natural warming phenomenon, also presents a risk to corals, Gudka said at a news conference at the UN’s COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.

It’s the latest dose of bad news for coral reefs, which are critical sources for seafood and tourism and often serve as buffers against coastal erosion and storms.

Sometimes dubbed “rainforests of the sea”, they have some of the world’s richest biodiversity and support a quarter of marine species as well as coastal communities and businesses.

Most of the world’s famous reef systems – including the Great Barrier Reef in Australia , the Coral Triangle in the Western Pacific Ocean and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System and the Red Sea coral reefs – are critically endangered, according to the assessment.

For its report, the IUCN used the “middle-of-the-road” scenario from the UN’s panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.

Its analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 square kilometres.

A week ago, another IUCN study in the journal Nature found that nearly 44 percent of reef-building coral species face an elevated risk of extinction due to climate change. A year ago, a survey found that harmful bleaching of the world’s coral had grown to include 84 percent of the ocean’s reefs, the most intense of its kind in recorded history.

Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world “are not yet lost”.

“Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events,” said Gudka. “Pockets of surviving, resilient coral reefs can still remain in the future, so we must do everything within our reach to set them up for success.”
